text: Capital Pride is an annual LGBT pride festival held in early June in Washington, D.C. It began as Gay Pride Day in 1975, a one-day block party and street festival organized by Deacon Maccubbin, owner of the LGBT bookstore Lambda Rising, on 20th Street NW between R and S Streets NW. The first event drew about 2,000 attendees and featured vending trucks with beer and soft drinks, as well as a dozen organizational booths. Notably, several D.C. City Council candidates attended and shook hands, signaling the growing political influence of the LGBT community. In 1979, the event moved to Francis Junior High School at 24th and N Streets NW, next to Rock Creek Park, and by 1981, a parade was added to the festival, which began at 16th Street NW and Meridian Hill Park, traveled along Columbia Road NW and Connecticut Avenue NW, and ended at Dupont Circle. Attendance grew to 11,000 in 1981, 15,000 in 1982, and 20,000 in 1983, reaching an estimated 28,000 by 1985. In 1984, the event expanded to a week-long series of meetings, speeches, dances, art exhibits, and parties. In 1983, the first woman and person of color was named Grand Marshal, and in 1984, the "Heroes of Pride" award was established for members of racial and ethnic minorities. Attendance fluctuated in the late 1980s, with only about 7,000 attending in 1986 and between 7,000 and 10,000 in 1987. Financial problems and concerns about inclusiveness led the P Street Festival Committee, formed in 1980, to disband in 1990 in favor of Pride of Washington. In 1991, the event moved to the week prior to Father's Day, hosted its first "Black Lesbian and Gay Pride Day" on May 25, expanded to over 200 booths, and included active-duty and retired military personnel in the parade; U.S. Air Force Captain Greg Greeley, who led the active-duty group, was temporarily protected from discharge due to his participation. The festival suffered financial losses due to rain and the absence of weather cancellation insurance, nearly going bankrupt. In 1995, One In Ten, a D.C.-based arts organization, took over planning and moved the street festival to Freedom Plaza near the White House. Attendance rose sharply, from about 25,000 in 1994 to over 100,000 in 1996. In 1997, Whitman-Walker Clinic (WWC) joined One In Ten as a co-sponsor and the event was renamed Capital Pride; the street festival moved to Pennsylvania Avenue NW between 14th and 10th Streets NW. Corporate sponsorships increased from $80,000 in 1998 to $247,000 in 1999. In 2000, WWC became the sole sponsor and the festival moved to Pennsylvania Avenue NW between 4th and 7th Streets NW, with the main stage positioned to have the U.S. Capitol in the background. In 2002, the parade was moved to early evening on Saturday while the festival remained on Sunday afternoon, and the number of parade contingents reached 200. In 2004, 100,000 people attended. Financial difficulties persisted, and in 2005, WWC requested an emergency $30,000 donation from the Human Rights Campaign and waived over $40,000 in fees from D.C. Mayor Anthony A. Williams; net proceeds were estimated at $30,000. Robert York, who had served as executive director since 1999, resigned unexpectedly in March 2005, followed by several staff resignations, and was replaced by David Mallory. Despite financial strain, Capital Pride attracted over 200,000 people in 2006, making it the fourth-largest gay pride event in the U.S., and included four major dance parties, a youth prom, a transgender dinner, and the first D.C. Leather Pride events. In 2007, WWC expanded oversight by forming the Capital Pride Planning Committee with 11 other local non-profits, and the city held its first Trans Pride and D.C. Latino Pride events. In 2008, WWC revealed a deficit of $32,795 for the 2007 festival on $167,103 in revenue, including $100,000 reimbursed for up-front expenses and $28,000 to other organizations. On January 11, 2008, WWC awarded the production rights to the Capital Pride Alliance, formed by members of the Planning Committee, which won over The Center, Westminster Presbyterian Church, and Jansi LLC. Capital Pride Alliance became the sole producer starting in 2009. The 35th anniversary in 2010 featured 60 events over 10 days and drew a record attendance of over 250,000 for the street festival. In 2011, organizers estimated attendance between 200,000 and 250,000 for both parade and festival. In 2012, the parade extended over 1.5 miles and drew about 100,000 spectators, with actual street festival attendance estimated at 250,000. In 2013, the Washington National Cathedral marched for the first time, led by Very Reverend Gary Hall, and attendance was reported at 100,000; the parade turned north on 14th Street NW, the festival started at noon and ended at 9:00 P.M., and a split occurred among D.C. Latino Pride organizers over fundraising and inclusion. In 2014, a U.S. Armed Forces color guard led the parade and retired the colors for the first time in American history, representing all branches of the military, with the Military District of Washington providing the guard; the parade attracted over 100,000 people and over 250,000 attended events during the week-long celebration. In 2015, the parade drew roughly 150,000 people. On June 8, 2019, a man with a BB gun caused a panic at the Dupont Circle parade, leading to a stampede and seven non-life-threatening injuries; police found no shots fired and arrested the man for possession of an illegal weapon and causing the panic. No Capital Pride was held in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the event was conducted virtually in 2021, resuming in-person events in 2022, including a parade and a festival where Vice President Kamala Harris surprised the audience. Originally called Gay Pride Day, the event changed its name to Gay and Lesbian Pride Day in 1981 and to Capital Pride in 2000.

A parade during Capital Pride drew roughly 150,000 people. On June 8, 2019, reports of gunfire at the Dupont Circle parade caused a panic, prompting people to flee through the streets; police determined no shots were fired, attributing the sounds to falling crowd-control barriers. A man with a BB gun was arrested for causing the panic and for possessing an illegal weapon; according to a police report, he pointed the BB gun at another person who was assaulting his female "significant other." Seven people were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries from the resulting stampede. No Capital Pride event was held in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the event was conducted virtually in 2021. Capital Pride resumed in-person events in 2022, including a parade and a festival where Vice President Kamala Harris surprised the audience. The event was originally called Gay Pride Day, changed its name to Gay and Lesbian Pride Day in 1981, and to Capital Pride in 2000. It was initially organized in 1975 by Deacon Maccubbin, owner of Lambda Rising Bookstore, with the help of bookstore employees, volunteers, and part-time executive director Bob Carpenter. Maccubbin and Lambda Rising hosted the event for the first five years until it grew to 10,000 attendees and spread over three blocks, making it too large for the available space; Maccubbin then sought an alternative location. In 1980, a group of community activists incorporated as the P Street Festival Committee, and Maccubbin transferred the event to them. Financial difficulties and concerns about lack of inclusiveness led the committee to disband in 1990, replaced by Pride of Washington. Further financial issues caused Pride of Washington to transfer the event to One In Ten in 1995. In 1997, One In Ten partnered with Whitman-Walker Clinic to co-produce the festival, and Whitman-Walker became the sole sponsor in 2000. Whitman-Walker turned the event over to the Capital Pride Alliance in 2008, which has continued to produce the festival. Although the Capital Pride Alliance was formed by 11 organizations, it now operates with a self-perpetuating board of directors. In 2005, an exhibit titled "Queering Sight—Queer Insight" opened at The Warehouse Gallery in the District of Columbia on June 3 and ran for a month. In 2006, Capital Pride was featured in the comedy film Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan. One In Ten sponsored a second exhibit on Capital Pride's history in 2007, installed at The Sumner School, a city-owned museum in a historic former school building in midtown D.C., which ran from March to June 2007. The New York Times in May 2014 called Capital Pride one "of the more notable Pride festivals and parades around the country."
